content: Biocompatible peritoneal dialysis (PD) solutions, such as those with neutral pH and low glucose degradation products (GDP), as well as icodextrin-based solutions, have been shown to positively impact certain patient outcomes. However, these findings are often based on studies of suboptimal quality. Recently, additional randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been conducted to evaluate the effects of these biocompatible solutions in PD patients. This review updates a prior analysis first published in 2014. The primary objective of this review was to assess the benefits and potential harms of biocompatible PD solutions compared to standard PD solutions in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis. The review included all RCTs and quasi-RCTs that compared biocompatible PD solutions (neutral pH, lactate-buffered, low GDP; neutral pH, bicarbonate-buffered, low GDP; and glucose polymer solutions like icodextrin) with conventional PD solutions. Studies involving amino acid-based solutions were excluded. The review incorporated data from 42 eligible studies involving 3,262 participants, including six new studies with 543 participants. Among these, 29 studies (1,971 participants) compared neutral pH, low GDP PD solutions with conventional glucose-based PD solutions, while 13 studies (1,291 participants) compared icodextrin with conventional glucose-based PD solutions. The risk of bias was assessed, with high risk noted in areas such as sequence generation, allocation concealment, attrition bias, and selective outcome reporting. Neutral pH, Low GDP PD Solutions vs. Conventional Glucose-Based PD Solutions: The use of neutral pH, low GDP PD solutions significantly improved the preservation of residual renal function (RRF). This was supported by high-certainty evidence from 15 studies involving 835 participants, with a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 0.19 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.05 to 0.33). This corresponds to a mean difference in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 0.54 mL/min/1.73 m² (95% CI 0.14 to 0.93). The preservation of RRF was observed across all follow-up durations, with greater benefits seen over longer follow-up periods. Neutral pH, low GDP PD solutions also improved the preservation of residual urine volume. High-certainty evidence from 11 studies involving 791 participants showed a mean difference of 114.37 mL/day (95% CI 47.09 to 181.65). There was low-certainty evidence suggesting that these solutions may have little to no effect on 4-hour peritoneal ultrafiltration. Data from nine studies (414 participants) indicated a standardized mean difference of -0.42 (95% CI -0.74 to -0.10), corresponding to a mean reduction in peritoneal ultrafiltration of 69.72 mL (95% CI 16.60 to 122.00 mL). Neutral pH, low GDP solutions may slightly increase the dialysate-to-plasma creatinine ratio (10 studies, 746 participants: mean difference 0.01, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.03). There was uncertainty regarding the impact of these solutions on peritonitis rates, hospitalizations, adverse events, or inflow pain. For example, one study (58 participants) reported a relative risk (RR) of 0.51 (95% CI 0.24 to 1.08) for inflow pain, but the evidence was inconclusive. Icodextrin vs. Conventional Glucose-Based PD Solutions: Icodextrin likely reduced episodes of uncontrolled fluid overload. Moderate-certainty evidence from two studies (100 participants) showed a relative risk of 0.30 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.59). Icodextrin significantly increased peritoneal ultrafiltration. Moderate-certainty evidence from four studies (102 participants) demonstrated a mean difference of 448.54 mL/day (95% CI 289.28 to 607.80). Icodextrin did not appear to compromise residual renal function. Low-certainty evidence from four studies (114 participants) showed a standardized mean difference of 0.12 (95% CI -0.26 to 0.49), corresponding to a mean creatinine clearance difference of 0.30 mL/min/1.73 m² (95% CI -0.65 to 1.23). There was no clear evidence that icodextrin affected urine output. Low-certainty evidence from three studies (69 participants) showed a mean difference of -88.88 mL/day (95% CI -356.88 to 179.12). The impact of icodextrin on adverse events, technique failure, or mortality remains uncertain, as the evidence from five studies (816 participants) was inconclusive. Conclusions: This updated review provides strong evidence that neutral pH, low GDP PD solutions improve the preservation of residual renal function and urine volume. These benefits may be linked to enhanced peritoneal solute transport and reduced peritoneal ultrafiltration, although the evidence for these mechanisms is of low certainty due to methodological limitations and heterogeneity among studies. Icodextrin was shown to increase peritoneal ultrafiltration and reduce episodes of uncontrolled fluid overload with moderate certainty. However, the effects of either neutral pH, low GDP solutions or icodextrin on peritonitis rates, technique survival, and patient survival remain uncertain. Further high-quality, adequately powered RCTs are needed to address these gaps in evidence.
